docs.preview:
# jsonwebtoken

| **Build**                                                                                                                               | **Dependency**                                                                                                         |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [![Build Status](https://secure.travis-ci.org/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken.svg?branch=master)](http://travis-ci.org/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken) | [![Dependency Status](https://david-dm.org/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken.svg)](https://david-dm.org/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken) |


An implementation of [JSON Web Tokens](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7519).

This was developed against `draft-ietf-oauth-json-web-token-08`. It makes use of [node-jws](https://github.com/brianloveswords/node-jws)

# Install

```bash
$ npm install jsonwebtoken
```

# Migration notes

* [From v8 to v9](https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/wiki/Migration-Notes:-v8-to-v9)
* [From v7 to v8](https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/wiki/Migration-Notes:-v7-to-v8)

# Usage

### jwt.sign(payload, secretOrPrivateKey, [options, callback])

(Asynchronous) If a callback is supplied, the callback is called with the `err` or the JWT.

(Synchronous) Returns the JsonWebToken as string

`payload` could be an object literal, buffer or string representing valid JSON. 
> **Please _note_ that** `exp` or any other claim is only set if the payload is an object literal. Buffer or string payloads are not checked for JSON validity.

> If `payload` is not a buffer or a string, it will be coerced into a string using `JSON.stringify`.

`secretOrPrivateKey` is a string (utf-8 encoded), buffer, object, or KeyObject containing either the secret for HMAC algorithms or the PEM
encoded private key for RSA and ECDSA. In case of a private key with passphrase an object `{ key, passphrase }` can be used (based on [crypto documentation](https://nodejs.org/api/crypto.html#crypto_sign_sign_private_key_output_format)), in this case be sure you pass the `algorithm` option.
When signing with RSA algorithms the minimum modulus length is 2048 except when the allowInsecureKeySizes option is set to true. Private keys below this size will be rejected with an error.

`options`:

* `algorithm` (default: `HS256`)
* `expiresIn`: expressed in seconds or a string describing a time span [vercel/ms](https://github.com/vercel/ms). 
  > Eg: `60`, `"2 days"`, `"10h"`, `"7d"`. A numeric value is interpreted as a seconds count. If you use a string be sure you provide the time units (days, hours, etc), otherwise milliseconds unit is used by default (`"120"` is equal to `"120ms"`).
* `notBefore`: expressed in seconds or a string describing a time span [vercel/ms](https://github.com/vercel/ms). 
  > Eg: `60`, `"2 days"`, `"10h"`, `"7d"`. A numeric value is interpreted as a seconds count. If you use a string be sure you provide the time units (days, hours, etc), otherwise milliseconds unit is used by default (`"120"` is equal to `"120ms"`).
* `audience`
* `issuer`
* `jwtid`
* `subject`
* `noTimestamp`
* `header`
* `keyid`
* `mutatePayload`: if true, the sign function will modify the payload object directly. This is useful if you need a raw reference to the payload after claims have been applied to it but before it has been encoded into a token.
* `allowInsecureKeySizes`: if true allows private keys with a modulus below 2048 to be used for RSA
* `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes`: if true, allows asymmetric keys which do not match the specified algorithm. This option is intended only for backwards compatability and should be avoided.



> There are no default values for `expiresIn`, `notBefore`, `audience`, `subject`, `issuer`.  These claims can also be provided in the payload directly with `exp`, `nbf`, `aud`, `sub` and `iss` respectively, but you **_can't_** include in both places.

Remember that `exp`, `nbf` and `iat` are **NumericDate**, see related [Token Expiration (exp claim)](#token-expiration-exp-claim)


The header can be customized via the `options.header` object.

Generated jwts will include an `iat` (issued at) claim by default unless `noTimestamp` is specified. If `iat` is inserted in the payload, it will be used instead of the real timestamp for calculating other things like `exp` given a timespan in `options.expiresIn`.

Synchronous Sign with default (HMAC SHA256)

```js
var jwt = require('jsonwebtoken');
var token = jwt.sign({ foo: 'bar' }, 'shhhhh');
```

Synchronous Sign with RSA SHA256
```js
// sign with RSA SHA256
var privateKey = fs.readFileSync('private.key');
var token = jwt.sign({ foo: 'bar' }, privateKey, { algorithm: 'RS256' });
```

Sign asynchronously
```js
jwt.sign({ foo: 'bar' }, privateKey, { algorithm: 'RS256' }, function(err, token) {
  console.log(token);
});
```

Backdate a jwt 30 seconds
```js
var older_token = jwt.sign({ foo: 'bar', iat: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 30 }, 'shhhhh');
```

#### Token Expiration (exp claim)

The standard for JWT defines an `exp` claim for expiration. The expiration is represented as a **NumericDate**:

> A JSON numeric value representing the number of seconds from 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z UTC until the specified UTC date/time, ignoring leap seconds.  This is equivalent to the IEEE Std 1003.1, 2013 Edition [POSIX.1] definition "Seconds Since the Epoch", in which each day is accounted for by exactly 86400 seconds, other than that non-integer values can be represented.  See RFC 3339 [RFC3339] for details regarding date/times in general and UTC in particular.

This means that the `exp` field should contain the number of seconds since the epoch.

Signing a token with 1 hour of expiration:

```javascript
jwt.sign({
  exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + (60 * 60),
  data: 'foobar'
}, 'secret');
```

Another way to generate a token like this with this library is:

```javascript
jwt.sign({
  data: 'foobar'
}, 'secret', { expiresIn: 60 * 60 });

//or even better:

jwt.sign({
  data: 'foobar'
}, 'secret', { expiresIn: '1h' });
```

### jwt.verify(token, secretOrPublicKey, [options, callback])

(Asynchronous) If a callback is supplied, function acts asynchronously. The callback is called with the decoded payload if the signature is valid and optional expiration, audience, or issuer are valid. If not, it will be called with the error.

(Synchronous) If a callback is not supplied, function acts synchronously. Returns the payload decoded if the signature is valid and optional expiration, audience, or issuer are valid. If not, it will throw the error.

> __Warning:__ When the token comes from an untrusted source (e.g. user input or external requests), the returned decoded payload should be treated like any other user input; please make sure to sanitize and only work with properties that are expected

`token` is the JsonWebToken string

`secretOrPublicKey` is a string (utf-8 encoded), buffer, or KeyObject containing either the secret for HMAC algorithms, or the PEM
encoded public key for RSA and ECDSA.
If `jwt.verify` is called asynchronous, `secretOrPublicKey` can be a function that should fetch the secret or public key. See below for a detailed example

As mentioned in [this comment](https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/issues/208#issuecomment-231861138), there are other libraries that expect base64 encoded secrets (random bytes encoded using base64), if that is your case you can pass `Buffer.from(secret, 'base64')`, by doing this the secret will be decoded using base64 and the token verification will use the original random bytes.

`options`

* `algorithms`: List of strings with the names of the allowed algorithms. For instance, `["HS256", "HS384"]`. 
  > If not specified a defaults will be used based on the type of key provided
  > * secret - ['HS256', 'HS384', 'HS512']
  > * rsa - ['RS256', 'RS384', 'RS512']
  > * ec - ['ES256', 'ES384', 'ES512']
  > * default - ['RS256', 'RS384', 'RS512']

report.overview: jsonwebtoken is Auth0's reference Node implementation of RFC 7519 JSON Web Tokens, published to npm as `jsonwebtoken` v9.0.3. It is a tiny, dependency-light library (three public functions — `sign`, `verify`, `decode` — plus three error classes) that wraps `jws` for the actual JWS signing/verification and layers on claim semantics (exp/nbf/aud/iss/sub/jti/nonce/maxAge), option schema validation, and a hard-won set of key-confusion defenses. What is distinctive is how much of the code is defensive rather than functional: roughly half of sign.js and verify.js is dedicated to coercing untrusted key material into `crypto.KeyObject`s, rejecting alg/key-type mismatches (the classic RS256→HS256 confusion attack), and enforcing a 2048-bit RSA modulus floor. It targets any Node service that issues or consumes JWTs, and ships both callback-async and synchronous-throwing modes of every entrypoint.

system_map.summary: This is a pure library with no server, no database, and no network I/O of its own — the only runtime boundary is the Node `crypto` module and the `jws` package. `index.js` is the whole public API surface: it re-exports `decode.js`, `verify.js`, `sign.js`, and the three error classes from `lib/`. Support modules in `lib/` are all single-purpose: feature-detection booleans gated on `process.version` via `semver`, a `ms`-backed timespan parser, and the asymmetric key/algorithm compatibility matrix. Build is nonexistent (plain CommonJS, no transpile); test is `mocha`, coverage is `nyc mocha --use_strict`, lint is `eslint .`. Deployment is npm publish driven by `semantic-release` in a two-workflow release dance on `master`.

claims.claim: `index.js` is the sole entrypoint and exports exactly six symbols: `decode`, `verify`, `sign`, `JsonWebTokenError`, `NotBeforeError`, `TokenExpiredError` — there is no class, no factory, no configuration object.

All cryptography is delegated to the `jws` package (`^4.0.1`): `jws.decode` in decode.js, `jws.sign`/`jws.createSign` in sign.js, and `jws.verify` in verify.js. This repo contains no hashing, HMAC, or signature code of its own.

The runtime dependency set is deliberately minimal and old-school: `jws`, `ms`, `semver`, and seven separately-published single-function lodash packages (`lodash.includes`, `lodash.isboolean`, `lodash.isinteger`, `lodash.isnumber`, `lodash.isplainobject`, `lodash.isstring`, `lodash.once`).

Node version capability is resolved at require-time, not call-time, by three boolean modules that `semver.satisfies(process.version, ...)`: `lib/psSupported.js` (`^6.12.0 || >=8.0.0`), `lib/asymmetricKeyDetailsSupported.js` (`>=15.7.0`), and `lib/rsaPssKeyDetailsSupported.js` (`>=16.9.0`).

PS256/PS384/PS512 are spliced into the algorithm allow-lists at module load only when `PS_SUPPORTED` — into `SUPPORTED_ALGS` at index 3 in sign.js, and appended to both `PUB_KEY_ALGS` and `RSA_KEY_ALGS` in verify.js.

The error hierarchy is hand-rolled ES5 prototype inheritance, not `class extends Error`: `JsonWebTokenError` calls `Error.call(this, message)` and manually sets `this.message`, and `NotBeforeError`/`TokenExpiredError` do `Object.create(JsonWebTokenError.prototype)` and add a `date`/`expiredAt` field.

`lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js` owns the key-type↔algorithm compatibility matrix (`allowedAlgorithmsForKeys` for `ec`/`rsa`/`rsa-pss`) and the ES-curve mapping (`allowedCurves`: ES256→prime256v1, ES384→secp384r1, ES512→secp521r1). It is the single shared gate called by both sign and verify.

`lib/timespan.js` is the only time-arithmetic module; it converts a `ms`-parseable string or a raw number into an absolute epoch-seconds timestamp, and returns `undefined` (not an error) for unparseable input, pushing error construction onto its three callers.

Developer commands are `npm test` (bare `mocha`), `npm run coverage` (`nyc mocha --use_strict`), `npm run lint` (`eslint .`), and `npm run update-changelog` (`conventional-changelog -p conventionalcommits -i CHANGELOG.md`). `npm run prepare` installs husky hooks.

CI is five GitHub Actions workflows: `test.yml` (PR-triggered matrix over Node 16/18/20/22/24), `commitlint.yml` (PR-triggered conventional-commit validation), `prepare-release.yml` and `release.yml` (both on push to master, mutually exclusive via a `chore(release):` head-commit-message guard), and `sca-scan.yml` (Snyk, via a pinned reusable workflow from `auth0/devsecops-tooling`).

Publishing is `semantic-release` configured in `.releaserc.json` on the `master` branch, with conventional-commits analysis, npm publish from repo root, a `prepareCmd` of `git diff --exit-code`, and a `verifyReleaseCmd` that runs a ReversingLabs `rl-wrapper` scan over the `npm pack` tarball before release.

The published npm tarball is narrowed by the `files` allow-list to `lib`, `decode.js`, `sign.js`, `verify.js` — tests, `bin/`, and workflows never ship. `.npmignore` additionally excludes `opslevel.yml`.

Repo ownership/routing is declared for Auth0 internal tooling: `CODEOWNERS` assigns everything to `@auth0/project-iam-protocols-engineer-codeowner` and `opslevel.yml` tags the repo to the `iam_protocols` owner.
`package.json` declares `engines.node >= 12`, but the test matrix only exercises Node 16 through 24 — the 12/14 support claim is unverified by CI.

feature_catalog.summary: The user-facing surface is three functions, each with a dual sync/async calling convention selected by whether a trailing callback is supplied. `sign` turns a payload plus key into a compact JWS, mapping option names onto registered claim names and computing time-based claims. `verify` is the security-critical path: it re-decodes, resolves a key (possibly via an async key-lookup callback for JWKS/kid workflows), enforces an algorithm allow-list, checks key/alg compatibility, verifies the signature, then runs seven independent claim checks. `decode` is the deliberately unauthenticated escape hatch. Twelve signing algorithms plus `none` are supported, and a set of explicit backwards-compatibility escape valves (`allowInsecureKeySizes`, `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes`) let callers opt out of the newer hardening.

claims.claim: `jwt.sign(payload, secretOrPrivateKey, [options, callback])` supports thirteen options validated by `sign_options_schema`: `expiresIn`, `notBefore`, `audience`, `algorithm`, `header`, `encoding`, `issuer`, `subject`, `jwtid`, `noTimestamp`, `keyid`, `mutatePayload`, `allowInsecureKeySizes`, `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes` — and rejects any key not in that schema with `"<key>" is not allowed in "options"`.

Four sign options are sugar that write registered claims, via the `options_to_payload` table: `audience`→`aud`, `issuer`→`iss`, `subject`→`sub`, `jwtid`→`jti`. Supplying both the option and the raw claim is an error (`Bad "options.<x>" option. The payload already has an "<claim>" property.`).

Non-object payloads (strings, numbers, Buffers) are supported for signing but reject the seven object-only options listed in `options_for_objects` with `invalid <opts> option for <typeof> payload`; a Buffer payload round-trips as its string form.
`mutatePayload: false` (the default) shallow-clones the payload with `Object.assign({}, payload)` before adding `iat`/`exp`/`nbf`, which is what makes signing a frozen or sealed payload work.
`options.encoding` (default `utf8`) is passed through to `jws`, so `{encoding: 'binary'}` produces a differently-encoded payload segment for non-ASCII characters.

`jwt.verify(token, secretOrPublicKey, [options, callback])` supports thirteen options: `algorithms`, `audience`, `complete`, `issuer`, `jwtid`, `ignoreExpiration`, `ignoreNotBefore`, `subject`, `clockTolerance`, `maxAge`, `clockTimestamp`, `nonce`, `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes`.

`secretOrPublicKey` may be a key-lookup function `(header, cb)` — the JWKS/`kid` integration point — but only when a callback is also supplied; otherwise verify fails with `verify must be called asynchronous if secret or public key is provided as a callback`.
Audience matching accepts a string, a `RegExp`, or an array of either, and matches if ANY token `aud` entry matches ANY expected audience — an any-to-any `some`/`some` cross product.

`clockTolerance` (seconds of slack) and `clockTimestamp` (override for "now") apply to `nbf`, `exp`, and `maxAge` uniformly; `clockTimestamp` must be a number or verify fails early with `clockTimestamp must be a number`.

`maxAge` is an independent expiry ceiling computed from `payload.iat`, requires a numeric `iat` (`iat required when maxAge is specified`), and cannot loosen `exp` — a token past `exp` still fails even with `maxAge: '1000y'`.
`complete: true` on either `verify` or `decode` returns `{header, payload, signature}` instead of the bare payload — this is how callers reach `kid` and `alg` for key selection.
`jwt.decode(token, options)` performs no signature verification at all, and silently swallows a `JSON.parse` failure on the payload — returning the raw string payload rather than throwing.

Unsigned (`alg: none`) tokens are supported on both sides but require explicit opt-in on verify: `please specify "none" in "algorithms" to verify unsigned tokens`, and passing a key alongside a signature-less token yields `jwt signature is required`.

Two named backwards-compatibility escape hatches exist and are documented as discouraged: `allowInsecureKeySizes` (permits RSA modulus < 2048) and `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes` (skips the `validateAsymmetricKey` gate).

data_flow.summary: There are exactly two input boundaries — the caller-supplied `(payload | jwtString, key, options)` tuple — and one output boundary, either a returned/thrown value or a `(err, result)` callback invocation. No state is owned across calls: the library is entirely stateless, with the only module-level mutable structures being the algorithm allow-list arrays built at require time. The central transform on both paths is key normalization: whatever the caller passes (string, Buffer, PEM, JWK-ish object) is funnelled through `crypto.createPrivateKey`/`createPublicKey` with a `createSecretKey` fallback into a `KeyObject`, and every downstream decision reads `key.type`, `key.asymmetricKeyType`, and `key.asymmetricKeyDetails` off that normalized object. Claim data flows one way on sign (options → payload properties → JWS) and one way on verify (JWS → decoded payload → claim assertions → returned payload).

claims.claim: On sign, key material normalization is a try/catch cascade: if not already a `KeyObject`, attempt `createPrivateKey(secretOrPrivateKey)`, fall back to `createSecretKey(Buffer.from(...))` for strings, and on double failure emit `secretOrPrivateKey is not valid key material`.

Verify mirrors that cascade with `createPublicKey` then `createSecretKey`, producing `secretOrPublicKey is not valid key material` — this is what converts a hostile object with a throwing `toString` into a clean error instead of arbitrary execution.

The JWS header is assembled by `Object.assign` with a fixed precedence: computed `{alg, typ, kid}` first (alg defaults to `HS256`, `typ` is `'JWT'` only for object payloads, `kid` comes from `options.keyid`), then `options.header` spread last so it can override any of them including `alg`.

A single `timestamp` value — `payload.iat || Math.floor(Date.now()/1000)` — is computed once and is the base for both `nbf` and `exp`, guaranteeing the three time claims are internally consistent within one sign call.

On verify, the token is parsed twice: once shallowly as `jwtString.split('.')` for arity (`jwt malformed` when length !== 3) and signature-presence checks on `parts[2]`, and once fully through `decode(jwtString, {complete: true})`.

`options` is defensively shallow-cloned on entry to verify (`Object.assign({}, options)`) specifically because the function later writes `options.algorithms` when the caller omitted it — caller-supplied objects are never mutated.

When `options.algorithms` is absent, the allow-list is derived from the normalized key: `secret`→HS_ALGS, `rsa`/`rsa-pss`→RSA_KEY_ALGS, `ec`→EC_KEY_ALGS, everything else→PUB_KEY_ALGS. This binds the accepted alg set to the key material, not to the token.

The token-supplied `header.alg` flows into `jws.verify(jwtString, decodedToken.header.alg, secretOrPublicKey)`, but only after passing the allow-list membership check and the key-type compatibility check — the ordering at lines 144→152→165 is the whole defense.

The verified `payload` object returned to the caller is the same object produced by `decode`, not a copy — all seven claim checks read from it without transforming it, so callers receive attacker-influenced data verbatim (the README explicitly warns to sanitize it).

Both functions funnel every error through a single sink — `failure(err)` in sign and `done(err, data)` in verify — which dispatches to `callback(err)` when async or `throw err` when sync, so sync and async modes are guaranteed to produce identical errors.

`decode` normalizes the payload channel: `jws.decode` may return a string payload, which `decode` opportunistically `JSON.parse`s and keeps only if the result is a non-null object — otherwise the string passes through unchanged.

`timespan(time, iat)` is the shared conversion from relative to absolute time on both paths: it feeds `payload.nbf`/`payload.exp` on sign and `maxAgeTimestamp` on verify, using `ms()` for strings and plain addition for numbers.
The only file-system reads in the entire repo are in tests, loading PEM fixtures from `test/*.pem` — the library itself performs zero file or network I/O.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows matter: module load (feature detection), signing, and verification. Module load is unusual in that it bakes Node-version capability into module-scope constants, so the same code path behaves differently on Node 14 vs Node 16 without any runtime branch. Signing is a long linear gauntlet of eleven guards before any crypto happens. Verification is the inverse-ordered gauntlet, and its ordering is load-bearing: algorithm allow-listing and key-type checks must both precede `jws.verify`. Both entry functions branch at the very end into callback vs synchronous return.

claims.claim: MODULE LOAD: `require('jsonwebtoken')` → index.js requires decode/verify/sign → sign.js requires `lib/psSupported` → `semver.satisfies(process.version, '^6.12.0 || >=8.0.0')` → if true, `SUPPORTED_ALGS.splice(3, 0, 'PS256','PS384','PS512')` executes at module scope. Algorithm support is therefore frozen at first require.

SIGN step 1-2: normalize arity (`typeof options === 'function'` → shift to callback), compute `isObjectPayload` as `typeof payload === 'object' && !Buffer.isBuffer(payload)`, then build `header` via `Object.assign`.
SIGN step 3-4: reject missing key unless `algorithm === 'none'`, then coerce to `KeyObject` via `createPrivateKey` → `createSecretKey` fallback.

SIGN step 5: enforce symmetry — `header.alg.startsWith('HS')` requires `key.type === 'secret'`; `/^(?:RS|PS|ES)/` requires `key.type === 'private'`; and for non-ES RSA algs, `asymmetricKeyDetails.modulusLength < 2048` is rejected (guarded by an `!== undefined` check for pre-Node-15 where the field is absent).

SIGN step 6-8: `validatePayload` (allowUnknown=true, checks only iat/exp/nbf are numbers) → clone payload unless `mutatePayload` → reject `exp`+`expiresIn` and `nbf`+`notBefore` double-specification → `validateOptions` (allowUnknown=false).

SIGN step 9-11: `validateAsymmetricKey(header.alg, key)` unless opted out → compute `timestamp` and apply `noTimestamp`/`iat` → `timespan` for `nbf` and `exp` → copy the four `options_to_payload` claims.

SIGN terminal branch (async): wrap callback in `once()`, then `jws.createSign({header, privateKey, payload, encoding})` with `.once('error', callback)` and `.once('done', ...)`; the done handler re-checks `signature.length < 256` as a pre-Node-15 proxy for the 2048-bit modulus rule.

SIGN terminal branch (sync): `jws.sign({header, payload, secret, encoding})` returns the token, followed by the identical `signature.length < 256` check which `throw`s rather than calling back. Both branches carry a `TODO: Remove ... once node 15+ is the minimum supported version`.

VERIFY step 1-4: arity normalization → clone options → build `done` (callback or throw-on-error closure) → validate `clockTimestamp`/`nonce`/`allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes` shapes → compute `clockTimestamp` → reject falsy or non-string `jwtString` → split into exactly 3 parts.

VERIFY step 5-6: `decode(jwtString, {complete: true})` inside a try/catch (returns `invalid token` if falsy), then choose `getSecret` — either the caller's key-lookup function or a trivial wrapper that immediately yields the static key. All remaining logic runs inside that callback.

VERIFY step 7: the three-way signature/key presence matrix — signature-without-key → `secret or public key must be provided`; key-without-signature → `jwt signature is required`; neither-plus-no-algorithms → `please specify "none" in "algorithms"`.

VERIFY step 8-10 (the security core, in this exact order): coerce key → derive default `algorithms` from key type → reject `header.alg` not in the list (`invalid algorithm`) → reject HS-alg-with-non-secret-key and RS/PS/ES-alg-with-non-public-key → `validateAsymmetricKey` → only then `jws.verify`.

VERIFY step 11 (claims, in order): `nbf` (type check then `> clockTimestamp + clockTolerance` → `NotBeforeError`) → `exp` (→ `TokenExpiredError`) → `audience` → `issuer` → `subject` → `jwtid` → `nonce` → `maxAge` (→ `TokenExpiredError('maxAge exceeded')`) → return payload or the `complete` triple.

KEY-CONFUSION TRACE: an attacker-forged `{alg: HS256, kid: rsaKeyId}` token presented with the legitimate RSA public key reaches line 148, where `header.alg.startsWith('HS') && key.type !== 'secret'` throws `secretOrPublicKey must be a symmetric key when using HS256` — before `jws.verify` is ever called. The test asserts this for both KeyObject and PEM forms.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is the strongest part of the repo: ~258 `it()` blocks across 30 mocha files in `test/`, backed by chai assertions, sinon fake timers, and 17 checked-in PEM fixtures covering RSA, RSA-PSS, EC (three curves), DSA, and deliberately-invalid keys. The signature move is `test/test-utils.js`, which runs every sign/verify twice — once sync, once async — under a frozen clock and asserts the two produce byte-identical tokens or deep-equal errors; this is why the sync/async parity invariant actually holds. Coverage is configured with hard nyc thresholds, but the CI workflow runs bare `mocha`, so those thresholds and eslint are never enforced on PRs. Test naming is split between a per-claim convention (`claim-*.test.js`, `option-*.test.js`) and older topic/regression files (`*.tests.js`, `issue_*.tests.js`).

claims.claim: The framework stack is mocha 5 + chai 4 + sinon 6, with `atob` used to independently decode base64url segments in encoding tests. There is no `.mocharc`, so mocha's default `./test/*.js` glob picks up every file in `test/`.

`test/test-utils.js` exports `signJWTHelper` and `verifyJWTHelper`, both of which freeze time with `sinon.useFakeTimers({now: Date.now()})`, run the sync call in a try/catch, then run the async call and assert equality of token or error before restoring the clock.

`expectEqualError` exists because chai does not deep-equal errors (the helper cites chaijs/chai#1009); it compares `message` and `name` explicitly plus every enumerable property, which is how `expiredAt`/`date` payloads on the error subclasses get verified.

Option/claim validation is tested exhaustively by table-driven loops over ~15 bad values (`true, false, null, -1.1, Infinity, NaN, ' ', '', [], ['foo'], {}, {foo:'bar'}` …), applied per-claim in `claim-exp.test.js`, `header-kid.test.js`, and siblings.
`test/claim-aud.test.js` is the largest test file at 436 lines and 36 `it()` blocks, reflecting that audience matching (string/regex/array cross-product) is the most branch-heavy claim check.

`test/jwt.asymmetric_signing.tests.js` is parameterized: it builds an `algorithms` map of RS256/ES256 (plus PS256 when `PS_SUPPORTED`) each with `pub_key`, `priv_key`, and an `invalid_pub_key` that is deliberately not the pair of `priv_key`, then runs the same describe block per algorithm.
Security regressions are explicitly locked in by `test/jwt.malicious.tests.js`: HMAC-with-RSA-key confusion (both KeyObject and PEM form) and the malicious-`toString` Buffer-impersonation RCE vector.

Historical bugs are pinned by dedicated regression files: `issue_70.tests.js` (PEM headers), `issue_147.tests.js` (signing an `Object.seal`ed payload), `issue_304.tests.js`, and `rsa-public-key.tests.js`.

`test/validateAsymmetricKey.tests.js` unit-tests the key-matrix module directly (not through sign/verify), including the no-key and no-algorithm short-circuit paths and the PS/curve branches gated on the feature-detection booleans.
nyc is configured with `check-coverage: true` and thresholds of 95% lines, 95% statements, 100% functions, 95% branches, excluding `./test/**` — a genuinely strict bar.

GAP: `test.yml` runs only `npm test` (bare mocha). Neither `npm run coverage` nor `npm run lint` appears in any workflow, so the nyc thresholds and the eslint ruleset are advisory only and can silently regress.

A known-broken case is parked rather than fixed: `it.skip('should work with none algorithm where secret is falsy')` in async_sign, annotated with a link to node-jws issue #62 — the async `alg: none` path with a falsy secret is untested and known not to work.

A coverage hole is deliberately carved out with `/* istanbul ignore next */` around the entire `ASYMMETRIC_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED` block in validateAsymmetricKey, with a comment explaining it would otherwise sink coverage on Node < 15.7.0 — meaning EC curve matching and RSA-PSS parameter checks are excluded from the coverage numbers.

Test fixtures include intentionally-bad keys used as negative cases: `invalid_pub.pem`, `ecdsa-public-invalid.pem`, `rsa-pss-invalid-salt-length-private.pem`, and `dsa-public.pem` (to assert `Unknown key type "dsa".`).

risk_map.summary: As a library whose entire job is security, nearly every line in verify.js is a security-sensitive path, and the ordering of its checks is the load-bearing invariant — any reordering that lets `jws.verify` run before the algorithm allow-list check reintroduces the classic JWT confusion attacks. The most concrete correctness defect is in sign.js's `options_to_payload` loop, where `return failure(...)` inside a `forEach` callback does not abort the enclosing function, so in async mode the callback can fire twice. Secondary risks cluster around Node-version-conditional code that CI does not fully exercise, deliberately silent error swallowing in `decode`, a very old eslint pinned at v4, and release workflows that handle several third-party secrets. Blast radius for any change here is unusually wide: this package sits in the dependency tree of a large fraction of Node auth stacks.

claims.claim: CORRECTNESS BUG: in the `options_to_payload` loop, `return failure(...)` only returns from the `forEach` arrow — the outer sign function continues. In async mode `failure` invokes the raw callback with an error at line 221, and since `callback` is not yet wrapped by `once()` (that happens at line 230), signing proceeds and the callback is invoked a second time with a valid token.

SECURITY-CRITICAL ORDERING: the allow-list check (`options.algorithms.indexOf(header.alg) === -1`), the key-type symmetry check, and `validateAsymmetricKey` all sit between `decode` and `jws.verify`. Any edit that moves `jws.verify` earlier, or that trusts `header.alg` before line 144, reopens the RS256→HS256 confusion class.

`options.header` is `Object.assign`ed LAST when building the sign header, so a caller passing `{header: {alg: 'none'}}` silently overrides `options.algorithm` — and the downstream key/alg checks then run against the overridden value. This is by design but is a sharp edge for callers who build headers from user input.

`decode` swallows all `JSON.parse` errors in an empty `catch (e) { }`, returning the raw string payload instead. Callers that assume an object back from `decode` will see a string on malformed tokens with no signal.

The `signature.length < 256` heuristic is an acknowledged stopgap for the 2048-bit modulus rule on Node < 15, duplicated in both the sync and async branches with matching `TODO: Remove ...` comments — a two-site invariant that can drift.

No source file uses `'use strict'`, so sloppy-mode semantics apply — e.g. `delete payload.iat` on a primitive string payload under `noTimestamp` is a silent no-op rather than a TypeError. Notably `npm run coverage` runs mocha with `--use_strict` while `npm test` does not, so the two commands exercise different semantics.

The EC curve check dereferences `key.asymmetricKeyDetails.namedCurve` without a null guard; it is protected only by the module-load `ASYMMETRIC_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED` semver boolean, and that whole block is excluded from coverage by `istanbul ignore next`.

The verified payload returned by `verify` is the same object `decode` produced, unsanitized and fully attacker-controlled in content; the README carries an explicit warning to treat it as user input, which implies downstream misuse is a known recurring problem.

`allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes: true` disables `validateAsymmetricKey` on both sign and verify, and a test asserts it lets an ES256-labelled token be processed with an RSA key — a documented footgun kept only for backwards compatibility.

`release.yml` handles six secrets (`PRODSEC_TOOLS_ARN`, `PRODSEC_TOOLS_USER`, `PRODSEC_TOOLS_TOKEN`, `RLSECURE_LICENSE`, `RLSECURE_SITE_KEY`, `SIGNAL_HANDLER_TOKEN`) and embeds credentials in a pip `--index-url`. Mitigations are in place — `persist-credentials: false`, `mask-aws-account-id: true`, SHA-pinned actions — but this job is the highest-value supply-chain target in the repo.

`prepare-release.yml` parses the next version out of semantic-release's human-readable stdout with `awk '/The next release version is/{print $NF}'` — a brittle coupling to log wording that would silently produce an empty version if the message text changes.

DEAD CODE: `bin/changelog` is a standalone conventional-changelog script with hardcoded `releaseCount: 19` and a commented-out `preset: 'jshint'`, but nothing references it — `package.json` and `prepare-release.yml` both go through the `update-changelog` npm script instead (per commit b924272).

STALE TOOLING: `eslint` is pinned at `^4.19.1` (with `ecmaVersion: 6` in the parser options, below the ES2018+ syntax the sources actually use), and `nsp@^2.6.2` — a long-deprecated security tool — remains a devDependency with no script invoking it.

The README still advertises Travis CI and david-dm badges even though CI has moved to GitHub Actions, and the TODO section admits `X.509 certificate chain is not checked` — a real, documented limitation for anyone using x509 PEMs as verification keys.

The `files` allow-list omits `index.js` despite it being `main`; npm force-includes the `main` file so the package works today, but the list is one refactor (e.g. moving the entry to `lib/`) away from shipping a broken tarball.

extension_points.summary: This library has no plugin system by design — a JWT implementation with third-party extension hooks would be a security liability. What it does have are a handful of declarative tables that are the intended edit sites for new capability, and one genuine runtime hook. The tables are the two option schemas and the `options_to_payload` map in sign.js, the four algorithm arrays in verify.js, and the `allowedAlgorithmsForKeys`/`allowedCurves` matrices in `lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js` — adding an algorithm means touching all three files coherently. The one caller-facing hook is verify's function-valued `secretOrPublicKey`, which is where JWKS clients plug in. Feature detection for new Node capabilities follows a one-file-per-boolean convention in `lib/`.

claims.claim: PRIMARY RUNTIME HOOK: `secretOrPublicKey` as a `(header, secretCallback)` function is the documented integration point for JWKS/`kid`-based key resolution; internally the static-key case is normalized into the same shape so there is exactly one code path after line 101.

Adding a new sign option means one entry in `sign_options_schema` with an `isValid` predicate and a `message` — the generic `validate(schema, allowUnknown, object, parameterName)` walker requires no other change, and unknown options are rejected because `validateOptions` passes `allowUnknown: false`.

`registered_claims_schema` is the parallel table for payload claims and is validated with `allowUnknown: true`, so arbitrary custom claims pass through while `iat`/`exp`/`nbf` are type-enforced — this asymmetry is the extension point for application-specific claims.

`options_to_payload` is a two-column map from option name to claim name; adding a new registered-claim shortcut is a one-line addition there, and the conflict-detection and copy logic applies automatically.

`options_for_objects` is the companion list declaring which options are meaningless for non-object payloads; any new object-only option must be added here too or it will be silently accepted on a string payload.

Algorithm support is defined in four arrays: `SUPPORTED_ALGS` (sign.js) and `PUB_KEY_ALGS` / `EC_KEY_ALGS` / `RSA_KEY_ALGS` / `HS_ALGS` (verify.js). A new algorithm requires edits in both files plus `allowedAlgorithmsForKeys`.

`allowedAlgorithmsForKeys` maps `asymmetricKeyType` → permitted `alg` values and is the single authority on key/algorithm pairing; an unrecognized key type throws `Unknown key type "<type>"`, so new key types must be registered here or they are rejected outright.
`allowedCurves` maps ES algorithms to required named curves and is the place to add a curve; it is consulted only under `ASYMMETRIC_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED`.

New Node-version feature gates follow a one-module-per-flag convention: a three-line file exporting `semver.satisfies(process.version, '<range>')`, consumed as a module-scope constant. Three such files already exist.

New error types extend the hierarchy by the ES5 pattern in `lib/NotBeforeError.js`: call `JsonWebTokenError.call(this, message)`, set `this.name`, add the payload field, then `prototype = Object.create(JsonWebTokenError.prototype)` and restore `constructor`. New types must also be re-exported from `index.js` to be reachable.

New verify-time claim checks slot into the linear block between `jws.verify` and the return, following the established `if (options.X) { if (payload.y !== options.X) return done(new JsonWebTokenError(...)) }` shape used by issuer/subject/jwtid/nonce.

Test convention for new options/claims: add a `test/option-<name>.test.js` or `test/claim-<name>.test.js` file that uses `testUtils.signJWTHelper`/`verifyJWTHelper` plus `asyncCheck`, so sync/async parity is enforced for free.

Release automation is itself extensible through `.releaserc.json`'s plugin array; the `@semantic-release/exec` entry is where additional pre-publish gates (currently `git diff --exit-code` and the ReversingLabs scan) would be added.

agent_handoff.summary: Treat this as a security library first and a JavaScript project second: the check ordering in verify.js and the guard cascade in sign.js are the product, and reordering them is never a safe refactor even when it looks like cleanup. Style is intentionally conservative CommonJS ES5/ES6 with no build step, no TypeScript, no async/await, and no strict mode — match it rather than modernize it. Read the four root JS files and `lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js` before touching anything; they are under 600 lines combined. Commits must be Conventional Commits because commitlint gates PRs via husky locally and a workflow in CI, and because semantic-release derives the version from them.

claims.claim: READ FIRST, in order: `index.js`, `sign.js`, `verify.js`, `decode.js`, `lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js`. That is the entire library — under 600 lines total — and everything else in `lib/` is a three-line helper.

RUN: `npm test` for the fast loop (mocha over `test/`), `npm run coverage` before proposing a merge (nyc enforces 95/95/100/95 and will fail the command), and `npm run lint` manually since no workflow runs it.

COMMIT FORMAT: Conventional Commits are mandatory. `.husky/commit-msg` runs `npx --no -- commitlint --edit $1` locally and `commitlint.yml` re-validates every commit in a PR range; `@commitlint/config-conventional` is the ruleset.

STYLE: 2-space indent enforced by both `.editorconfig` and the eslint `indent` rule; no semicolon rule, no quote rule. eslint is pinned at v4 with `ecmaVersion: 6`, so avoid syntax newer than ES2015 in new code paths or the lint run will fail to parse.

TRAP — check ordering: in verify.js, lines 144 (allow-list), 148-152 (key-type symmetry), and 154-160 (key/alg matrix) must all remain before line 165 (`jws.verify`). Moving or short-circuiting any of them is a vulnerability, not a refactor.

TRAP — dual calling convention: every change to sign or verify must work identically in sync (throws) and async (callback) mode. `test/test-utils.js` asserts byte-equality of tokens and deep-equality of errors across the two, so a one-sided fix will fail loudly.

TRAP — `return` inside `forEach`: the existing `options_to_payload` loop already has this bug (a `return failure(...)` that does not abort the function). Do not copy that pattern into new claim-copy logic, and be aware that fixing it changes observable async callback behavior.

TRAP — Node-conditional code: three `semver.satisfies` booleans are evaluated at module load. Code behind `ASYMMETRIC_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED` and `RSA_PSS_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED` will not execute on your local Node unless it is new enough, and is excluded from coverage — verify such changes against the CI matrix (16/18/20/22/24), not just locally.

SAFE EDIT BOUNDARY: adding a claim check, a validated option, or a test is low-risk and well-patterned. Changing key coercion (`createPrivateKey`/`createPublicKey`/`createSecretKey` cascades), the algorithm arrays, or `validateAsymmetricKey` is high-risk and touches published security behavior.

DO NOT EDIT casually: `CHANGELOG.md` is generated by `npm run update-changelog` during the prepare-release workflow, and `package.json` `version` is bumped by `npm version --no-git-tag-version` in that same workflow. Hand-editing either will conflict with the release automation.

RELEASE SHAPE: pushing to master triggers `prepare-release.yml`, which opens a `release/vX.Y.Z` PR titled `chore(release): X.Y.Z`; merging that PR matches the `startsWith(..., 'chore(release):')` guard and triggers `release.yml` to run `npx semantic-release`. The two workflows are mutually exclusive by that guard.

New public API or option changes must be reflected in `README.md`, which is the only user documentation and is structured as `jwt.sign` / `jwt.verify` / `jwt.decode` / Errors & Codes / Algorithms supported.
Any PR touching `lib/`, `sign.js`, or `verify.js` will require review from `@auth0/project-iam-protocols-engineer-codeowner` — the CODEOWNERS glob is `*`, so every path is covered.

Do not add PEM fixtures casually: 17 already exist covering RSA, RSA-PSS (valid and invalid salt length), EC on three curves, DSA, and invalid public keys — reuse them via the `loadKey(filename)` helper convention.

Security vulnerabilities must not be filed as GitHub issues — the README directs them to Auth0's Responsible Disclosure Program. An agent discovering one should report it to the user rather than opening a public issue.

report.agent_prompt:
You are working on `jsonwebtoken` (auth0/node-jsonwebtoken), the reference Node.js implementation of RFC 7519 JSON Web Tokens, currently v9.0.3 on branch `master`. This is a security library published to npm and depended on by a very large slice of the Node auth ecosystem — assume wide blast radius for every change.

ARCHITECTURE. It is plain CommonJS with no build step, no TypeScript, and no `'use strict'`. `index.js` exports six symbols: `sign`, `verify`, `decode`, and the error classes `JsonWebTokenError`, `NotBeforeError`, `TokenExpiredError`. The three functions live in root-level `sign.js`, `verify.js`, `decode.js`. All actual cryptography is delegated to the `jws` package; this repo contributes claim semantics, option validation, and key-confusion defenses. `lib/` holds only small helpers: three `semver.satisfies(process.version, ...)` feature-detection booleans (`psSupported`, `asymmetricKeyDetailsSupported`, `rsaPssKeyDetailsSupported`), a `ms`-backed `timespan.js`, the three error classes, and `validateAsymmetricKey.js` which owns the key-type↔algorithm matrix and the ES curve mapping.

HOW IT WORKS. Both `sign` and `verify` accept an optional trailing callback; with it they are async and yield `(err, result)`, without it they are synchronous and throw. Every error routes through one sink (`failure()` in sign, `done()` in verify) so the two modes produce identical errors — `test/test-utils.js` enforces this by running both and asserting byte-equal tokens or deep-equal errors under a frozen sinon clock. Both paths normalize whatever key material the caller passes into a `crypto.KeyObject` through a `createPrivateKey`/`createPublicKey` → `createSecretKey` try/catch cascade, then make every subsequent decision from `key.type`, `key.asymmetricKeyType`, and `key.asymmetricKeyDetails`.

THE CRITICAL INVARIANT. In `verify.js`, these run in this exact order and must stay that way: derive default `algorithms` from key type (L132-142) → reject `header.alg` not in the allow-list (L144) → reject HS-alg-with-non-secret-key and RS/PS/ES-alg-with-non-public-key (L148-152) → `validateAsymmetricKey` (L154-160) → only then `jws.verify` (L165). This ordering is what blocks the RS256→HS256 key-confusion attack; `test/jwt.malicious.tests.js` pins it. Never move `jws.verify` earlier or trust `header.alg` before the allow-list check. Claim checks (nbf, exp, aud, iss, sub, jti, nonce, maxAge) follow afterward.

EXTENSION POINTS. New sign options go in `sign_options_schema`; new registered-claim shortcuts go in `options_to_payload` (and `options_for_objects` if object-only). New algorithms require coordinated edits to `SUPPORTED_ALGS` (sign.js), the four arrays in verify.js, and `allowedAlgorithmsForKeys` in validateAsymmetricKey.js. The only caller-facing hook is verify's function-valued `secretOrPublicKey` for JWKS/kid lookup.

KNOWN TRAPS. (1) The `options_to_payload` loop uses `return failure(...)` inside a `forEach`, which does not abort the function — in async mode this can invoke the callback twice. Do not replicate the pattern. (2) Code behind the Node-version booleans will not execute on older runtimes and is excluded from coverage via `istanbul ignore next`. (3) `decode` swallows JSON.parse errors silently. (4) `npm test` and `npm run coverage` differ — the latter adds `--use_strict`.

COMMANDS. `npm test` (mocha, ~258 tests in `test/`), `npm run coverage` (nyc, thresholds 95/95/100/95 — enforced by the command but NOT by CI), `npm run lint` (eslint v4, also not run by CI — run it yourself). Commits must be Conventional Commits; husky's `commit-msg` hook and a PR workflow both enforce this, and semantic-release derives versions from them. Do not hand-edit `CHANGELOG.md` or the `version` field — both are automated. Update `README.md` for any user-visible API change. Report security findings to the user, not to the public issue tracker.
